section.title: Paul Defends His Ministry
section.sectionRationale: The tone of the letter shifts sharply. Having appealed for the collection, Paul now turns to answer the critics who despise him, opening the great defense of his apostleship that runs to the end of the letter. He answers not with self-promotion but by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, insisting that the weapons of his warfare are not fleshly but carry divine power to demolish strongholds and take every thought captive to obey Christ.
section.thesis: True ministry is waged not with the weapons of the flesh but with the divine power of the gospel, which demolishes strongholds and takes every thought captive to Christ; and the servant of Christ commends himself not by measuring himself against others but by boasting only in the Lord, for the approved one is the one whom the Lord commends.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the weapons of our warfare that have divine power to demolish strongholds; the charge that Paul's letters are weighty but his presence weak; and boasting only in the Lord within the field God has assigned.

units.label: Weapons with divine power
units.note: we do not wage war according to the flesh

verses.text: Now by the mildness and gentleness of Christ, I appeal to you, I, Paul, who am humble when face to face with you, but bold when away.
I beg you that when I come I may not need to be as bold as I expect toward those who presume that we live according to the flesh.
For though we live in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh.
The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the flesh. Instead, they have divine power to demolish {{ochyroma|strongholds}}.
We demolish {{logismos|arguments}} and every presumption set up against the knowledge of God; and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ.
And we will be ready to punish every act of disobedience, as soon as your obedience is complete.

units.label: Weighty letters, unimpressive presence
units.note: what we are in word we will be in deed

verses.text: You are looking at outward appearances. If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, he should remind himself that we belong to Christ just as much as he does.
For even if I boast somewhat excessively about the authority the Lord gave us for building you up rather than tearing you down, I will not be ashamed.
I do not want to seem to be trying to frighten you by my letters.
For some say, “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account.”
Such people should consider that what we are in our letters when absent, we will be in our actions when present.

units.label: Boast only in the Lord
units.note: the one whom the Lord commends is approved

verses.text: We do not dare to classify or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves. When they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they show their ignorance.
We, however, will not boast beyond our limits, but only within the field of influence that God has assigned to us, a field that reaches even to you.
We are not overstepping our bounds, as if we had not come to you. Indeed, we were the first to reach you with the gospel of Christ.
Neither do we boast beyond our limits in the labors of others. But we hope that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you will greatly increase as well,
so that we can preach the gospel in the regions beyond you. Then we will not be boasting in the work already done in another man’s territory.
Rather, “Let him who {{kauchaomai|boasts}} boast in the Lord.”
For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

ochyroma.gloss: A stronghold, fortress, or fortified place. Paul pictures the proud reasonings raised against the knowledge of God as enemy fortifications. The gospel is the siege weapon that has divine power to tear them down. The image is of spiritual conquest, not by human cleverness or force, but by the truth of Christ breaking through every entrenched defense of the human heart.

logismos.gloss: A reasoning, argument, or calculation of the mind. Here it names the lofty speculations and proud thoughts that set themselves up against the knowledge of God. Paul does not merely refute ideas; he takes every thought captive to make it obedient to Christ. The battlefield of true ministry is the mind, where rebellious reasonings are brought into submission to the Lord.

kauchaomai.gloss: To boast, glory, or take pride in something. The word runs through these chapters as Paul's opponents boast in themselves. Quoting Jeremiah, Paul redirects all boasting to its only fitting object: let the one who boasts boast in the Lord. Legitimate glorying is never self-commendation but confidence in what God has done, so that the approved servant is the one whom the Lord commends, not himself.

basic.context: Paul turns from the collection to defend himself against critics at Corinth who sneer that he is bold in his letters but timid in person. He answers with startling gentleness, appealing by the meekness of Christ, yet with real authority. His ministry is a war, but not one fought with worldly weapons; its power is divine, able to pull down the proud arguments raised against God and to capture every thought for Christ.
basic.hermeneutics: Chapters 10 to 13 are Paul's sustained, sometimes ironic, defense of his apostleship. Read this passage as the opening salvo: he answers accusations about his manner and authority, then relocates all boasting from self to the Lord. The military language of verses 3 to 5 is about spiritual conflict, the demolition of ideas and pretensions, not physical or political power.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul says the gospel has power to demolish every ochyroma, stronghold, the fortress of proud reasoning. He tears down every logismos, argument, that exalts itself against God, taking every thought captive to Christ. And he ends by redirecting all kauchaomai, boasting, away from self and to the Lord.
basic.typology: Paul's warfare fulfills the pattern of Israel's battles, now transposed to the spiritual realm; the true weapon is the word of God, sharper than any sword. The meekness and gentleness of Christ, in which Paul appeals, reflects the Servant who did not break a bruised reed yet whose word carries the authority of heaven.
basic.christ: Christ is the pattern and the power of this ministry. Paul appeals by His meekness and gentleness, mirroring the Lord who was gentle and lowly yet spoke with divine authority. Christ is the one to whom every thought is taken captive, the knowledge of God that proud reasonings resist, and the Lord in whom alone the servant may boast.
basic.god: God is the one who supplies weapons of divine power, who assigns each servant his field, and who alone commends the approved worker. Paul's confidence rests not in himself but in the God who gave him authority for building up the church. The passage guards God's glory by refusing all self-promotion: boasting belongs to the Lord.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 6 describes the armor of God and the sword of the Spirit. Jeremiah 9 is the source of let him who boasts boast in the Lord. Matthew 11 shows Christ gentle and lowly in heart. Hebrews 4 calls the word of God living and active, sharper than any sword.
basic.oneStory: The Bible tells of God overcoming rebellion, not by worldly might but by His word and His Servant. Paul wages that same war at Corinth, pulling down proud reasonings with the gospel and taking every thought captive to Christ. True authority in God's kingdom looks like the meekness of Christ and boasts only in the Lord.

context.literary:
Chapter 10 opens the last major division of the letter, and it does so with a sudden, deliberate change of voice. The first words are 'I, Paul,' stressed with an emphasis he rarely uses, and the sentence that follows plays two Pauls against each other: the one 'humble when face to face' and the one 'bold when away.' Paul takes his critics' label and turns it into the opening of his argument. Verses 1 to 6 speak of gentleness and war together, which makes the paragraph hard to categorize and easy to remember.

The section divides into three movements. Verses 1 to 6 describe the nature of the warfare: its weapons, its targets and its timing. Verses 7 to 11 answer charges about outward appearance, authority and the gap between his letters and his presence. Verses 12 to 18 take up boasting, first by refusing to join a competition of self-commendation and then by explaining the limits of his field. The last verse ties these together with a single principle: the approved one is the one whom the Lord commends.

The writing is full of irony and word-play. Paul says that his critics 'look at outward appearances,' and then he answers with the language of measurement and rule. Words for boasting, commending and comparing appear so often that the passage reads as a theology of how not to praise oneself. The unusual density of military terms in verses 3 to 6, war, weapons, strongholds, captives, punishment, is balanced by building language in verse 8, 'building you up rather than tearing you down.' Paul's authority is both demolition and construction, and the second purpose governs the first.

Finally, the passage faces forward. It sets up the 'fool's speech' of chapters 11 and 12, in which Paul boasts reluctantly, and the warning of chapter 13 that he will come a third time. Chapter 10 is therefore the doorway into the hardest section of the letter.
context.historical:
Corinth rewarded polished speakers. Public rhetoric was a career and a form of entertainment, and visiting teachers were judged on their delivery, their appearance and their ability to promote themselves. Paul had come in a very different way, 1 Corinthians 2:1-5, determined to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and Him crucified. The taunt of verse 10, that his letters are weighty and his presence unimpressive, shows how his critics measured him. They wanted a man of visible power, and they found him unimpressive.

The critics themselves are not named. In later chapters Paul calls them 'super-apostles' and warns of false apostles who disguise themselves as servants of righteousness, 11:5, 11:13-15. They appear to have been outsiders who had come to Corinth with letters of commendation, 3:1, and who boasted of Hebrew heritage and of their ministry, 11:22-23. Their weapon was comparison: they set their credentials against Paul's and found him wanting. Verse 12 says they commended themselves, measuring themselves only against themselves.

Military language was a natural source of images in a city under Roman control. The Corinthians knew what a fortified citadel was and what it meant to take captives and to demand obedience. Paul uses the images to describe spiritual war with a sharp reversal: the weapons are not swords, and the captives are thoughts.

The reference to his 'field,' verses 13 to 16, reflects the apostle's missionary strategy. He deliberately preached where Christ had not been named, Romans 15:20, so that he would not build on another man's foundation. Corinth lay inside the field God had given him, since he had been the first to bring the gospel there, verse 14. The rival teachers, by contrast, were entering a field planted by someone else and claiming credit for it. The history of church planting that Luke records in Acts 18:1-11 stands behind that claim.
context.canonical:
Paul's warfare language belongs to a long Old Testament tradition in which the LORD is a warrior who fights for His people and whose weapons are not human. Zechariah 4:6 says it is not by might or power but by the Spirit, and Isaiah 11:4 describes the Messiah striking the earth with the rod of His mouth. Paul's own fullest description of the Christian's armor is in Ephesians 6:10-18, where the sword is the word of God, and Hebrews 4:12 says that word is living and active, sharper than any double-edged sword.

The language of tearing down and building up is taken from the prophets. Jeremiah was appointed to uproot and tear down and also to build and plant, Jeremiah 1:10, and Paul claims the second half of that commission in verse 8 and again at the end of the letter, 13:10. The identification of the sphere of ministry and the refusal to build on another's work finds its parallel in Romans 15:20 and 1 Corinthians 3:10.

The closing quotation draws on Jeremiah 9:23-24 and Paul also uses it in 1 Corinthians 1:31. In both places it comes at a turning point where he is dismantling human claims. The point that approval comes from the Lord, verse 18, stands beside Romans 2:29 and 1 Corinthians 4:5, where the Lord will bring to light the purposes of the heart and each will receive his commendation from God.

The meekness and gentleness of Christ in verse 1 recalls Matthew 11:29, where Jesus calls Himself gentle and humble in heart, and the prophecy of Zechariah 9:9 of the king who comes lowly and riding on a donkey. The chapter thus links the Old Testament warrior, the gentle Messiah and the apostle who imitates both.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted the Corinthians to see that the charges against him had a hidden premise, namely that real ministry must look impressive, and he intended to destroy that premise. He does not defend himself by showing that he can be bold. He says that his gentleness is Christ's own gentleness, and then he states what his boldness will be like if he must use it: it will be in action what it was in letters, verse 11.

He also meant to put the Corinthians on notice. The tenderness of verse 1 and the threat of verse 6 belong together. He would rather not use severity, verse 2, and he gives them time to come to obedience first, verse 6. This is not blustering. It is a pastor warning a church that has begun to listen to the wrong voices.

His deepest aim was to change the way the church measures ministry. The Corinthians were comparing teachers by outward standards. Paul invites them to compare nothing and to ask instead what the Lord is doing, what field God has given, and whom the Lord commends. In doing so he takes the measure out of human hands.

The first hearers would have understood that this was not a quarrel over personal honor. It concerned the gospel itself. If ministry is validated by self-promotion and polish, then the cross, which looked like weakness, would count for nothing. Paul's defense of himself is a defense of the cross as the way God works in the world.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The details of this chapter are descriptive: the particular charges, the particular rivals and the particular field that God had assigned to Paul. We should not assume that every church leader has an apostle's authority to punish disobedience, verse 6, or that every field of ministry is as Paul describes it. The authority he speaks of was given to him as an apostle, and it was for building up, not tearing down.

The prescriptive parts are the principles that come through. The weapons of Christian ministry are spiritual, whatever the conflict, and they work through truth, prayer and the gospel. Every thought is to be brought into obedience to Christ, which is a call to the life of the mind as well as of the heart. Leaders should be gentle as Christ is gentle, even when they are firm. They should not measure themselves by comparison with others or boast of work that belongs to others. And the believer's boast is the Lord.

A caution about verse 5 is useful. It is sometimes used as a general slogan about controlling one's thoughts, and it does bear on that. In context it speaks first of arguments and pretensions raised against the knowledge of God. Taking thoughts captive is part of the gospel's conquest of the mind, and it is done with the weapons of truth and not with force or manipulation.

debates.question: What are the 'strongholds' and 'arguments' that Paul demolishes?

views.label: Human ideologies and proud reasoning
views.case: The text speaks of 'every presumption set up against the knowledge of God' and of 'every thought.' This favors a broad reading in which the strongholds are patterns of thought, in the individual and in society, that resist the gospel.

views.label: The specific case of the Corinthian rivals
views.case: Paul is in the middle of a defense of his apostleship, and the immediate targets are the claims of the rivals and the Corinthians' loyalty to them. The war metaphor is therefore applied to a particular conflict about the truth of the gospel and of his ministry.

views.label: Spiritual powers working through ideas
views.case: Others point to Ephesians 6:12 and read the strongholds as the work of spiritual forces that stand behind false teaching. The passage then describes a conflict that is real in the unseen realm as well as in the mind.

debates.bearing: The views are not mutually exclusive. Paul's own words connect arguments, thoughts and obedience, and the particular conflict at Corinth is one instance of the larger struggle. The weapons are the same in each case: the truth of the gospel and the power of God.

debates.question: Who are the opponents behind Paul's defense?

views.label: Jewish Christian missionaries from outside
views.case: The mention of Hebrews, Israelites and descendants of Abraham in 11:22 suggests teachers with a Jewish background who had arrived with letters of commendation and who valued heritage and visible credentials.

views.label: Missionaries linked to the Jerusalem apostles
views.case: Some suppose that Paul's 'super-apostles' were the Jerusalem leaders or their emissaries. Yet Paul's tone toward Peter and John elsewhere is respectful, and he treats the intruders in chapter 11 as false apostles, which makes it unlikely that he means the Twelve.

views.label: A mixed group drawn by Corinthian culture
views.case: A third view holds that the opponents were a varied group of itinerant teachers who adopted the rhetoric and self-promotion prized in Corinth, and that Paul meets them on the ground of their own culture without labeling them a single party.

debates.bearing: The text does not give us a full identification. What matters is the pattern: teachers who commend themselves and measure by outward standards. That pattern can recur in any age, and Paul's answer to it holds whoever the original opponents were.

debates.question: Are chapters 10 to 13 part of the original letter or a separate, earlier severe letter?

views.label: An integral part of one letter
views.case: The shift in tone can be explained by a pause in writing, by fresh news, or by Paul's turn to the minority that still opposed him. The manuscripts present 2 Corinthians as one letter.

views.label: Fragments of a distinct severe letter
views.case: Some scholars see chapters 10 to 13 as a separate letter, possibly the painful letter mentioned in 2:3-4, later joined to chapters 1 to 9. The very different mood is the main reason.

debates.bearing: The message stands either way. The simplest reading takes the letter as one document, in which Paul closes by confronting directly what he has so far addressed more gently.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 names two qualities of Christ, prautes and epieikeia, usually 'meekness' and 'gentleness.' The first is strength under control, the word Jesus uses of Himself in Matthew 11:29. The second suggests fairness and a willingness not to press every right. Paul appeals by these, using the verb parakaleo, 'I urge,' which usually carries the sense of coming alongside. The critics read gentleness as weakness, and Paul answers by placing it at the center of his authority. He also quotes the insult directly: humble, tapeinos, 'lowly,' was a term of contempt in Corinth for someone with no standing.

The verb in verses 2 and 3 is peripateo, 'to walk,' a common word for the conduct of life. Paul says that some think he walks 'according to the flesh,' kata sarka. In verse 3 he plays on the phrase: he walks in the flesh, en sarki, since he is a human being, but he does not wage war according to the flesh, kata sarka. The preposition makes the whole difference. The verb for 'wage war' is strateuomai, a soldier's service, and in verse 4 the noun 'warfare' is the related strateia.

In verse 4 the weapons are dynata to theo, literally 'powerful to God' or 'mighty before God.' The phrase is a Hebrew-style idiom that can mean 'divinely powerful,' as the BSB renders it, and it can also suggest that the weapons are powerful in God's sight. The word 'demolish,' kathairesis, in the same verse is the noun for tearing down, and the same word is used again in verse 8 when Paul says his authority is for building up rather than tearing down. The verb of verse 5, kathaireo, is the matching form. One word thus joins the two uses of authority.

Verse 5 names logismoi, 'reasonings,' and hypsoma, a 'high thing' or 'height' raised up. It is a picture of proud elevation against the knowledge of God. The captives are noemata, 'thoughts' or 'purposes,' the same word used in 2:11 of Satan's designs, and the verb aichmalotizo, 'to take captive,' belongs to the vocabulary of conquest. The goal is hypakoe, 'obedience,' and the obedience is to Christ. This is the word that governs the passage: the obedience of the Corinthians in verse 6 is the goal of the whole war.

In verse 6 the word for punishment is ekdikeo, often rendered 'avenge' or 'bring justice.' Paul is ready to enforce discipline, but only after the obedience of the many is complete. Verses 12 to 18 revolve around the terms synkrino, 'to classify,' enkrino, 'to count among,' and synistemi, 'to commend.' The measure of verse 13 is the Greek metron tou kanonos. A kanon is a rule or measuring line, so the phrase can mean 'the limit of the measuring rule' or 'the sphere assigned.' It gives the English word 'canon.' Verse 16 speaks of the regions 'beyond you,' ta hyperekeina. In verse 17 the verb kauchaomai, 'boast,' is the same verb as in verse 15, and the quotation in verses 17 and 18 closes the loop with dokimos, 'approved,' a word for metal that has been tested and found genuine.

typology.type: The weapons of the LORD's warfare, 1 Samuel 17:45-47
typology.fulfillment: David met Goliath with a sling and the name of the LORD, and told the giant that the battle belongs to the LORD, who does not save by sword or spear. Paul's weapons in verse 4 are the same in kind: not what the world counts as strength, but God's power. The escalation in Christ is that the battle is against the powers and the thoughts that hold people captive, and its weapon is the word of the cross, 1 Corinthians 1:18. The type falls short because David's victory was over a single champion, while the victory of the gospel takes people captive in order to free them.

The great fortified city fell without a siege engine, at the sound of trumpets and the shout of the people, so that the stronghold came down by God's act. Paul's image of demolishing strongholds draws on the same biblical pattern of walls brought down by the power of God. In Christ the walls are the defenses of human pride and the barrier between peoples, Ephesians 2:14. The comparison is a loose correspondence, not an explicit citation, and it falls short because Jericho was a city of stone, while the strongholds of verse 4 are in the mind.

typology.type: Moses, meek and yet commissioned with authority, Numbers 12:3
typology.fulfillment: Moses is called the most humble man on earth, and he is also the one through whom God spoke to Pharaoh and Israel. The pairing of meekness and authority is the very pairing Paul claims in verse 1. The escalation in Christ is that the Lord Jesus is greater than Moses, Hebrews 3:3, and His gentleness, Matthew 11:29, is joined to all authority in heaven and on earth, Matthew 28:18. The type falls short in that Moses was a faithful servant in the house, whereas Christ is the Son over it.

typology.type: Jeremiah, appointed to tear down and to build, Jeremiah 1:10
typology.fulfillment: The prophet received a commission with two edges: to uproot and tear down, and to build and plant. Paul sees his own apostolic authority in the same terms and says it is given for building up. In Christ both movements are accomplished at once, for the cross tears down sin and death and builds a people. Paul is a servant of that, and not the center of it. The correspondence is real, though Paul does not name Jeremiah 1:10 in this chapter, and the comparison should be held with care.

study.christ:
The chapter begins in Christ's own character. 'By the meekness and gentleness of Christ' is a strange way to start a defense of apostolic authority, and Paul chose it deliberately. The Corinthians had been looking for someone who looked strong. Paul points to the Lord who was gentle and lowly in heart, Matthew 11:29, and who rode into Jerusalem on a donkey, Matthew 21:5. Christ's power has never taken the form that the world expects, and a servant who imitates Him will not either.

Gentleness is not weakness. The same Christ who was meek is the one before whom every thought is to be brought captive. Verse 5 speaks of obedience to Christ, which only makes sense if Christ is Lord over the mind and over every claim. His gentleness is a chosen way of exercising authority, not an absence of it. Philippians 2:5-11 holds the same two things together: the one who took the form of a servant is the one at whose name every knee will bow.

The conflict itself is Christ's. The strongholds of verse 4 are the same powers that the Lord confronted in His ministry and at the cross. At the cross He disarmed the rulers and authorities, Colossians 2:15, and in His resurrection He was declared Son of God in power. Every demolition that Paul undertakes is an extension of that victory. The weapons are divine because they are His, and the war is won in advance.

Verse 7 contains a quiet claim worth noticing. The rivals boasted that they belonged to Christ, and Paul answers that he belongs to Christ just as much as they do. To belong to Christ is the basic fact of Christian identity, and no one can claim a higher belonging. Nothing in the passage allows a ministry to claim extra status over fellow believers by comparing credentials.

Finally, Christ is the content of the boast. The quotation at the end, 'Let him who boasts boast in the Lord,' is applied by Paul in 1 Corinthians 1:30-31 to Christ, who has become our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. To boast in the Lord is to boast in Christ crucified, Galatians 6:14. The criterion of verse 18, that the approved person is the one the Lord commends, is also fulfilled in Christ, who was commended by the Father at His baptism and transfiguration, Matthew 3:17 and Matthew 17:5. The Lord Jesus never commended Himself, John 8:54, and was approved by the one who sent Him. That is the pattern for every servant.
study.god:
The God of this passage is a God of divine power who works through human weakness. The weapons have 'divine power,' literally power in relation to God, verse 4. Paul does not trust his own strategy, his speaking skill or his authority as a leader. He relies on the One who demolishes strongholds. That does not make the apostle passive, but it puts every effort of his into a frame where God is the actor.

He is a God who assigns. The 'field' in verse 13 is one that God has assigned, using the language of measurement. Boundaries in ministry are not set by ambition or competition but by what the Lord has given. This is a thought about divine providence on a small scale: He allots to each servant a portion of the work and a place to do it. The right response is to work within that portion with gratitude and to rejoice in what others are given.

He is a God who is gentle as well as strong. The appeal of verse 1 is made in the name of Christ's meekness, and the Son shows us the Father's character. The Old Testament presents the LORD as a warrior and also as a shepherd who gathers lambs in His arms, Isaiah 40:11. Paul's practice of withholding severity until it is needed reflects the God of Exodus 34:6, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion.

He is a God who searches thoughts. Verse 5 is about 'every thought,' and the whole apparatus of human reasoning is in His view. Psalm 139:2 says that He discerns our thoughts from afar. A God who commands that thoughts be brought into obedience is a God who has a claim on the inner life as well as on outward behavior.

He is also a God who alone commends. Verse 18 closes the chapter with a theological principle: self-praise proves nothing, and God's approval is the only approval that matters. This is the doctrine of God as judge turned into a pastoral comfort. The servant who is misunderstood, unimpressive and criticized can rest in the Lord's verdict, 1 Corinthians 4:3-5. For worship, the passage leads us to pray with confidence for the demolition of what exalts itself against God, to be content in the place He has given, and to refuse every kind of boasting that takes credit that belongs to Him.

crossReferences.note: The believer's armor: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. It spells out what Paul means in verse 4 by weapons that are not of the flesh, and it shows that the struggle is not against flesh and blood.

The source of the closing quotation. Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong in his strength, nor the rich in his riches, but let the one who boasts boast in knowing the LORD. Paul applies it to himself and to the whole matter of ministry credentials.

God chose the foolish, the weak and the lowly so that no one may boast before Him, and the verse ends with the same quotation, 'Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.' It shows that the principle of verse 17 was the foundation of the Corinthians' own calling.
Jesus says He is gentle and humble in heart. The words describe the meekness that Paul invokes in verse 1 and show that the character he appeals to is one that Christ Himself claimed.

The word of God is living and active, sharper than any double-edged sword, and it discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart. It explains how a word can be a weapon that reaches thoughts and demolishes proud reasoning, as in verse 5.

The LORD touches Jeremiah's mouth and appoints him to uproot, tear down, build and plant. Paul's claim in verse 8 that his authority is for building up and not for tearing down echoes this twofold commission.

Paul's ambition is to preach where Christ has not been named, so that he will not build on another's foundation. It matches verses 15 and 16, where he refuses to boast in another man's territory and looks to regions beyond Corinth.

Paul writes while absent so that when present he need not be severe in using the authority the Lord gave him for building up. This is the closing restatement of verse 8, and it makes plain that the whole defense is for the sake of the church.

Paul says it matters little to him if he is judged by the Corinthians, since it is the Lord who judges, and that each will receive his commendation from God. It is the same principle as verse 18, stated in a calmer setting.

Not by might nor by power but by My Spirit, says the LORD. The word to Zerubbabel states in a single line the principle behind the weapons of verse 4, that God's work is done by His Spirit and not by human force.

study.oneStory:
The Bible presents a long war between God and the powers that oppose Him, and it keeps showing that the war is won in an unexpected way. In Genesis 3:15 the seed of the woman will crush the serpent's head even though He will be wounded in the heel. Israel is delivered from Egypt by God's hand while the people stand still, Exodus 14:13-14. Gideon's army is reduced to three hundred, Judges 7, and Zechariah is told that it is not by might. Over and over the LORD fights in a manner that humbles human strength.

The prophets also look for a king who is gentle. Isaiah 42:1-4 describes the servant who will not break a bruised reed and who brings justice to the nations, and Zechariah 9:9 describes the king riding on a donkey. In Jesus these two lines meet. He is both the conqueror of Isaiah 11 and the servant of Isaiah 53, and His victory is won on a cross. Paul has learned to see all of his ministry in that light.

The theme of boasting also runs throughout the story. In Genesis 11 humanity builds a tower to make a name for itself, and in Jeremiah 9 the LORD tells Israel that the only fitting boast is in knowing Him. The prophet's call is the other side of the story of Babel. In the gospel the person who knows God is the person who has been known by Him, and no one has anything to boast about but the cross, Galatians 6:14.

The church in Corinth stands between these stories. It is a young congregation tempted to judge ministry by the standards of the city, and Paul is teaching it to see by the standard of the kingdom. Their own loyalty to Christ is at stake, and so is the way the gospel is understood by the watching world.

The story ends with a conquest that has no violence. In Revelation 19:11-16 the rider on the white horse is called Faithful and True, and the sword that comes from His mouth is His word. Every proud height will have been brought low, and every thought captive in the best sense, because every mind will finally be free to know Him. The saints who boasted only in the Lord will hear His commendation, and the people who once measured themselves by one another will find that the Lord's approval is the only one that lasts.

quiz.q: By what does Paul make his appeal to the Corinthians in verse 1?

options.text: By the mildness and gentleness of Christ.
options.note: Paul grounds even his boldness in the Christlike manner of gentleness.

options.text: By the weight of his apostolic office alone.
options.note: He has authority, but he appeals first by the meekness of Christ.

options.text: By the eloquence of his speech.
options.note: His critics said his speaking was of no account; that is not his appeal.
He appeals gently, though he is ready to act if needed.

quiz.q: What are the weapons of Paul's warfare, and what do they accomplish?

options.text: Not weapons of the flesh, but weapons with divine power to demolish strongholds.
options.note: Verse 4 states the nature and power of gospel warfare.

options.text: Powerful arguments that win by human cleverness.
options.note: The power is divine, not merely rhetorical skill.
These are weapons of the flesh, which Paul refuses.
The warfare is spiritual, aimed at proud reasonings, not people.

quiz.q: What does Paul say about every thought in verse 5?

options.text: Every thought is taken captive to make it obedient to Christ.
options.note: The battlefield is the mind, brought into submission to Christ.

options.text: Every thought should be freely explored without limits.
options.note: Paul aims to capture thoughts for Christ, not leave them free.

options.text: Only sinful actions, not thoughts, matter to God.
options.note: Paul specifically addresses thoughts and reasonings.
Proud reasonings set against God are exactly what must be demolished.

quiz.q: According to verses 17 and 18, who is truly approved?

options.text: The one whom the Lord commends, who boasts in the Lord.
options.note: Approval comes from the Lord, not from self-commendation.

options.text: The one who commends himself most persuasively.
options.note: Self-commendation is exactly what Paul rejects.

options.text: The one who measures himself against other leaders.
options.note: Comparing oneself to others shows ignorance, Paul says.

options.text: The one with the most impressive presence.
options.note: Outward appearance is what Paul's critics valued, not the Lord's approval.

questions: Paul appeals by the meekness and gentleness of Christ even while defending his authority. Where are you tempted to defend yourself with worldly weapons rather than a Christlike spirit?

The weapons of our warfare have divine power to demolish strongholds. What entrenched arguments or false beliefs, in yourself or around you, need the power of the gospel rather than mere human persuasion?
Paul speaks of taking every thought captive to obey Christ. What would it look like, practically, to bring your thought life under the obedience of Christ this week?
Paul's critics valued impressive presence and polished speech. Where do you find yourself judging ministry, or being judged, by worldly standards rather than faithfulness to Christ?
Let him who boasts boast in the Lord. What are you quietly boasting in, and how would boasting in the Lord instead reshape your confidence?

translationNotes.note: The mildness and gentleness of Christ translates two words for meekness and forbearing kindness.
Strongholds renders ochyroma, a fortress; the metaphor is of gospel siege warfare against the fortifications of proud human reasoning.
Field of influence translates a term for an assigned measure or sphere of ministry.
Let him who boasts boast in the Lord quotes Jeremiah 9:24; Paul redirects all glorying from self to the Lord who alone commends His servants.
